analysis.one_liner: Directs FDA to study why interchangeable biologic drugs are substituted less easily than generics.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to study making interchangeable biologic drugs easier to substitute died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Biologic drugs (like insulin and many specialty medicines) can be very expensive, and cheaper copies called "interchangeable biologics" can be swapped in at the pharmacy without a new prescription — but that happens far less often than with ordinary generic pills. This bill would order the Department of Health and Human Services to study whether differences between the two approval systems are slowing that substitution, report to Congress within 12 months, and update the FDA's "Purple Book" — the official list that tells pharmacists what can be substituted — to better line the systems up. It would not itself change any approval rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take expensive biologic medicines, who could see more pharmacy-level substitution of cheaper copies and lower out-of-pocket costs if the study leads to smoother substitution rules. Biosimilar makers would also benefit from a clearer, more familiar substitution framework. Any benefit is indirect, since the bill only commissions a study and a bookkeeping update.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to complete, within 12 months, a study of whether differences between the system for designating a biologic 'interchangeable' and the system for rating generic drugs as 'therapeutically equivalent' are reducing substitution of interchangeable biologics, and to report the results to Congress.

Directs the FDA to update the Purple Book — the list that tells pharmacists which products can be substituted — so that the way substitutability is communicated for biologics better matches the way generic therapeutic-equivalence ratings are communicated, with the stated goal of 'minimizing any impediments to the substitution' while keeping the two approval pathways distinct.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic manufacturers, whose high prices depend partly on fewer of their products being substituted at the pharmacy. The study and Purple Book changes would apply public pressure toward easier substitution, though the bill imposes no direct new costs, fees, or rules on them.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not itself change any rule or lower any price — it only orders a study and an update to a reference list, so patients would see no direct benefit even if it had passed.
The study deadline of 12 months after enactment carries no penalty and no follow-up requirement, so Congress would have been free to ignore the results.

Making biologic substitution look more like generic substitution is a good-faith point of controversy: biologics are large, complex molecules that are harder to copy exactly than small-molecule pills, which is why Congress set up a stricter 'interchangeable' standard in the first place; critics of loosening it argue the distinct pathway protects patient safety, and the bill explicitly preserves the two separate pathways.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential upside for patients on high-cost biologics is real but modest and indirect — smoother substitution could mean lower prices over time, but this bill is only a first diagnostic step, not a price fix. The costs are minimal and fall on brand-name drug makers who benefit from the current friction. As a low-cost, bipartisan information-gathering bill, it is hard to fault on design; the problem is that even this modest step never received consideration.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which passed it down to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, a Republican, introduced the Biologics Competition Act of 2023 on March 24, 2023, with three cosponsors: Reps. Barragán (D), Murphy (R), and Kuster (D).
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and a week later, on March 31, 2023, it was referred to that committee's Subcommittee on Health.
No further action was taken for the rest of the 118th Congress — the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name biologic manufacturers are better off, since the status quo — a stricter, less-used substitution pathway that limits pharmacy-level swaps of their products — stays untouched. Patients on expensive biologics gained nothing, but the bill was only a study, so the loss is small.

for.name: Reps. Nanette Barragán (D), Gregory Murphy (R), and Ann Kuster (D)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it two Democratic and two Republican supporters.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers, R)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 24, 2023 and passed it to the Health Subcommittee on March 31; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican and drew a 2-2 split of Democratic and Republican cosponsors; no one publicly opposed it — it simply was never taken up.

industries.note: The bill targets a key way brand biologics keep premium prices: substitution at the pharmacy is rare under the current interchangeable-biologics system. A study and Purple Book update aimed at 'minimizing impediments' to substitution points in the opposite direction, though it imposes no direct rule change on them.
A substitution system that works more like the familiar generic system would enlarge their market. Their interest in easier substitution runs alongside patients' interest in lower-cost copies.
